newsitem.title: UK: Pound hit by surprise fall in UK manufacturing.
newsitem.headline: Pound hit by surprise fall in UK manufacturing.

text.p: A surprise drop in UK manufacturing output for May knocked the pound back over a pfennig as the data took some of the steam out of interest rate rise expectations and prompted a bout of profit-taking, dealers said.
Sterling dropped back below the 2.94 marks level and also eased more than half a cent to levels below $1.69 after the figures.
The extent of the drop was limited though as traders continued to bet on a rate rise to result from this week's meeting of the Bank of England's policy-making council.

"The pound has clearly come under pressure from these very weak data, which have cooled the heightened rate rise expectations," said James McKay, internatinal economist at Paine Webber. "It's unlikely to prevent a rate hike this week though but the likelihood of a 50 basis points hike might have lessened."
The BOE's policy-making council meets on Wednesday and Thursday.

"They (the monetary policy committee) will be looking at consumer demand which is far too strong," said Glenn Davies, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais. "The pound has come off sharply on the figures but the interest rate differentials remain very attractive," he said.
Manufacturing output tumbled 1.1 percent in May, the largest monthly fall since June 1993. Industrial output was down 0.9 percent. The market had expected increases on both measures.

The pound was at 2.9355/65 marks at 0930 GMT, down from 2.9506 before the data and from 2.9592/02 in late European trading on Friday. Against the dollar, it was at $1.6838/45 from $1.6914 ahead of the data and $1.6856/66 at the previous close.
The Bank of England trade-weighted index was at 103.2, down from 104.0 at Friday's close.

Sterling surged to a fresh 70-month high at 2.9650 marks last week after the fiscal tightening in the 1997/98 budget from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown was seen as insufficient to rein in strong consumer demand.

This leaves higher interest rates as the only means to take up the slack, economists said. Fuelled by strong economic growth, Britain already has the highest base lending rates of the major world economies at 6.5 percent.

In the European Union, only Ireland and Greece have higher rates. Interest rates in continental Europe are expected to remain low as a result of sluggish economic growth, high unemployment and tight fiscal policies aimed at meeting criteria for European monetary union membership.
The Office for National Statistics said export levels held up and there was little evidence sterling was having an effect.
But analysts said today's data highlighted the trend of Britain's twin-track economy of robust consumer demand but sluggish manufacturing exports.
Sell stops were triggered on sterling's break below 2.9460, with strong support seen at 2.93, traders said.

The currency is in a consolidation phase after its rampant rise last week, which took it through the 2.95 marks level, its old central parity rate in the European exchange rate mechanism during Britain's membership from 1990 to 1992.
